disease_info: Bulimia nervosa is characterized by recurrent episodes of binge eating accompanied by a sense of loss of control, followed by inappropriate compensatory behaviors such as vomiting, fasting, overexercise, or misuse of medications to prevent weight gain. Self-evaluation is typically unduly influenced by body weight and shape, and individuals often oscillate between restrictive dieting and episodes of overeating. The course can be chronic or intermittent, with symptoms waxing and waning in response to stress, transitions, and changes in interpersonal or work demands. It is distinguished from binge-eating disorder by the presence of regular compensatory behaviors and from anorexia nervosa, binge-purge type, by the absence of significantly low body weight.

narrative.stressor: About six months before she presented, Ariana was promoted to lead a new life-and-health sales initiative at her agency, on top of her long-standing property and casualty book. The added responsibilities meant longer hours on the road, more client dinners, and constant performance metrics, all while she tried to keep up with volunteering and organizing the Bucyrus Harvest Festival. As her schedule tightened and she spent more time eating on the go, she found herself swinging between strict dieting to "look professional" at networking events and episodes of eating large amounts of comfort food alone late at night after long days. Over roughly four months this pattern intensified, spilling into workdays when she would skip lunch then overeat in her car between appointments, and she finally sought psychiatric help after a humiliating moment when she was too preoccupied with her eating pattern during a client meeting to follow the discussion, making her fear she was jeopardizing her reputation and her mentoring role with younger agents.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Once I start eating, especially at night after work, I feel like I can’t stop or control how much I’m eating.”

narrative.stressor: Martin’s firm began encouraging senior managers to plan gradual retirement, and about five months ago he shifted to a reduced schedule with the understanding that he would fully retire within two years. The loss of daily structure and the sudden extra time at home, combined with his long-standing tendency to get absorbed in creative projects, led him to alternate between periods of skipping proper meals while painting or working on models and then eating large, improvised meals late in the evening. Over four months, he responded to these episodes by imposing rigid rules on himself—like long, compensatory exercise walks and strict next-day restrictions—which only made his eating feel more out of control when he inevitably broke those rules. He came to psychiatric care after his primary doctor, noticing weight fluctuations and hearing about his increasingly extreme cycles of "making up" for what he ate, urged him to talk with a mental health professional before the pattern worsened as he approached full retirement.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep swinging between eating way too much and then trying to ‘make up for it’ with these harsh rules and routines, and it’s starting to take over my days.”

narrative.stressor: Joan’s symptoms escalated during her second full year of teaching, when her school introduced a new literacy curriculum with aggressive benchmark targets that played directly into her competitive drive. In the months leading up to spring assessments, she began staying late most evenings to refine lesson plans, often skipping regular meals and then eating large amounts of food alone in her apartment while trying to unwind with knitting or reading. As her sense that she had to maintain a certain appearance as a young, high-performing teacher grew—especially after a casual comment from a colleague about "summer body goals" in the staff room—her preoccupation with her weight and shape intensified, and she started organizing her days around what she saw in the mirror and what the scale said. Over four months she increasingly avoided social activities, postponed planned quiet trips, and eventually sought psychiatric care after realizing that her mood, self-worth, and even her willingness to stand in front of the class were being dictated by how she felt about her body on any given day.
narrative.chief_complaint: “How I feel about my body and weight is completely controlling how I see myself and how I function at school.”
